explication:
<explanation>
1. Identify the project type and purpose  
   - Hetty is a full-stack HTTP toolkit for security research. It runs as a single CLI-launched process that:  
     • Acts as a man-in-the-middle (MITM) HTTP proxy.  
     • Hosts a GraphQL API.  
     • Serves a Next.js-based web admin interface.  
   - Users point their browser or tools at the proxy, then use the web UI to inspect, edit, replay, and search HTTP traffic.  

2. Analyze the file structure  
   - Top-level “cmd/hetty”: Go code for CLI entrypoint, proxy instantiation, server wiring.  
   - “pkg/…”: Core Go libraries for proxy (pkg/proxy), database (pkg/db/bolt), filtering (pkg/filter), request logging (pkg/reqlog), scope and sender logic, Chrome helper integration.  
   - “pkg/api” + “gqlgen.yml”: GraphQL schema, generated types, resolvers back the web UI.  
   - “admin/”: Next.js React app (TypeScript) powered by Apollo-GraphQL, with features under “features/…”, shared components under “lib/…”, and pages under “pages/…”.  
   - Config/build files: Dockerfile, Makefile, gqlgen.yml, Go module files, workflows for CI.  

3. README insights  
   - Confirms triad of proxy / GraphQL / web UI.  
   - Notes embedded Bolt DB for per-project storage.  
   - Describes key features: intercept, scope, sender, HTTP request logs, project isolation.  

4. How to create the system design diagram  
   a. Main components (draw as distinct boxes):  
      • CLI Process (“hetty” binary)  
      • MITM Proxy module (pkg/proxy/*)  
      • GraphQL API server (pkg/api + gqlgen)  
      • Bolt DB storage (pkg/db/bolt)  
      • Next.js Admin UI client (admin/)  
      • Apollo GraphQL client (admin/src/lib/graphql)  
      • External browser or HTTP client (pointing at proxy)  
      • Target web servers on the Internet  
      • Optional Chrome launcher helper  
   b. Relationships and interactions (use directional arrows):  
      • HTTP client → Proxy → Target server (and back).  
      • Proxy writes request/response data to Bolt DB via pkg/db.  
      • Proxy consults pkg/filter, pkg/scope to decide intercept/rules.  
      • Proxy intercepts flow and emits events consumed by GraphQL resolvers.  
      • Admin UI (browser) ↔ HTTP(S) ↔ GraphQL API (same process) ↔ DB.  
      • Admin UI sends GraphQL queries/mutations to manage projects, scope, logs, intercept settings, and to trigger send/replay.  
      • CLI flags configure DB path, certs, listening address.  
   c. Architectural patterns and design principles:  
      • Single-process, modular Go application with layered packages.  
      • GraphQL façade over internal domain logic (API layer separated from proxy core).  
      • Embedded key-value store (Bolt) for multi-project isolation.  
      • Next.js SSR/CSR hybrid delivering React SPA powered by Apollo.  
      • Contexts and hooks (React) for state management.  
      • Filter AST/parser pipeline for scope/intercept rules.  
   d. Key technologies, frameworks, libraries:  
      • Go + gqlgen + net/http for proxy and API.  
      • Bolt DB for storage.  
      • Next.js, React, TypeScript, Apollo Client for admin UI.  
      • GraphQL schema & codegen for client/server types.  
      • Docker for containerized deployment.  
      • GitHub Actions, goreleaser for CI/CD and releases.  

5. Guidelines for tailoring to this full-stack application  
   - Draw clear separation between backend (Go process: proxy + API + DB) and frontend (Next.js + Apollo) layers.  
   - Highlight the MITM proxy data flow separately from GraphQL management flow.  
   - Show database interactions as a distinct persistence layer beneath proxy and API.  
   - Illustrate API as the single integration point for the UI and any external CLI commands (e.g., cert management).  

6. Diagram elements to include  
   - Box and label each component (Proxy, API, DB, UI, Client, External servers).  
   - Directional arrows for data flow (HTTP traffic vs GraphQL calls).  
   - Color-code or shape-code by component type (e.g., green for network, blue for storage, orange for UI).  
   - Annotations for key protocols (HTTP, HTTPS, WebSockets if any, GraphQL over HTTP).  
   - Docker icon if depicting container deployment.  

7. Emphasis on detail  
   - Break down packages into functional modules in your diagram (e.g., proxy/intercept, proxy/modify, reqlog, scope, sender).  
   - Show how the filter AST/parser pipeline sits in the intercept path.  
   - Include the Chrome-launcher helper as an optional automation component.  
   - Capture the lifecycle of a request: entry → filter/scope → store → intercept → modify → forward → log.  

By following these guidelines, you’ll produce a comprehensive, accurate, and tailored system diagram that captures Hetty’s full-stack architecture and operational workflows.  
</explanation>
